archetype.name: Pocket Passer (intermediate attacker)
archetype.definition: A rhythm thrower who rarely leaves the pocket and makes his living on the 10-to-30-yard window, especially over the middle, rather than on his legs or on volume underneath.

report.headline: A real downfield passer now, still undone by sacks and dead-end short throws.
report.take:
Year four Bryce Young is a different passer from the one who ranked 51st in EPA per play as a rookie. His 0.071 EPA per dropback sits 21st of 49, his yards per attempt is up 0.83 on last season, and his bad-throw rate has fallen to 12.7%, the cleanest of his career. He has also stopped being a runner: scrambles are only 2.1% of his dropbacks and his rushing is down 7.6 yards a game from last year. This is a pocket passer now, and the pocket is where the case for and against him lives.

What drives the good version is the ball traveling past 10 yards. On throws of 10-plus air yards he is at 0.688 EPA per attempt with a +8.1 CPOE, and that depth group alone accounts for 70.1 EPA. Throws in the middle of the field have produced 0.662 EPA per play, a 74.3% completion rate and no interceptions. Tetairoa McMillan (0.376 EPA per target on 72 targets) and Darren Waller are the main beneficiaries. Everything under 10 yards nets out slightly negative. Throws behind the line have cost 25.8 EPA at a -13.4 CPOE, which points as much to the screen and swing design as to him. The 274.6 passing yards a game, fourth in the league, is partly a byproduct of Carolina throwing more than almost anyone (third in pass rate over expected) behind a defense that ranks last in hit rate and sack rate and keeps putting him in shootouts.

The numbers hide two things. The 0-3 slide and -0.179 EPA per dropback over the last three games is really a two-game collapse. Tampa Bay has the No. 2 defense now, and Green Bay came on four days' rest. In those games his intended air yards shrank to 6.8 and 4.7, and the sacks piled up, 5 and 6. Against Denver he bounced back with a +11.1 CPOE and three touchdowns. The quieter, more structural problem is that drives die when the offense gets behind the chains. On third down he has taken 12 sacks and converted just 33.8% against an average of 8.4 yards to go. His 7.8% sack rate ranks 30th, and his pressure-to-sack rate has climbed back above the 20.9% he posted last season. In close fourth quarters he is at -0.239 EPA per play.

He is heading toward a useful but streaky middle-tier starter. He is dangerous when the line lets him hold the ball long enough to throw over the linebackers, and he is easy to strangle when it doesn't. With starting guard Damien Lewis out, the protection question becomes more pressing, not less.

strengths.title: Wins in the 10-plus-yard window
strengths.body: Nearly all of his value comes on throws beyond 10 air yards, where he completes passes well above expectation despite the harder throws. This lines up with career-best ball placement, so it reads as skill growth rather than luck, though the deep slice is only 34 attempts and will cool somewhat.

strengths.title: Owns the middle of the field
strengths.body: Over the middle he has been close to flawless: high completion rate, big EPA, no picks. That is where McMillan and Waller do their damage, and it suggests he is reading leverage and throwing with anticipation between the hashes. Outside throws to the left have been roughly break-even, so the middle is the engine.

strengths.title: Volume built into the offense
strengths.body: Carolina throws far more than game situations call for, and its defense keeps games high-scoring. That combination props up his yardage and touchdown totals regardless of efficiency. Because it comes from team identity rather than hot play, it should hold all year.

concerns.title: Sacks kill drives on third down
concerns.body: Twelve of his sacks have come on third down, where he converts only a third of the time, often in long yardage. He holds the ball a bit longer than average to let routes develop downfield, and his pressure-to-sack rate has crept up from last year. This is partly the price of his downfield style and partly line play. It is a real, recurring cost, and it gets worse with a starting guard out.

concerns.title: Dead short game behind the line
concerns.body: Throws behind the line of scrimmage have been a steady drain, completed well below expectation and adding up to a large negative EPA. Everything under 10 yards nets out slightly below zero. Some of that is screen design and execution around him, but it means the offense has no easy-yardage floor when the deep shots are taken away.

concerns.title: Shrinks against good fronts
concerns.body: In the Tampa Bay and Green Bay losses his intended air yards collapsed and the sacks and interceptions spiked. Good defenses can take away his intermediate game and leave him checking down. The Denver rebound shows it isn't permanent, but his floor against top units is low.

trend.note: Strong opening fortnight, a choppy middle, then a two-game crater against Tampa Bay and Green Bay before a sharp Week 9 bounce-back against Denver. The last-three window looks worse than his current form.

nextGame.headline: Saints' leaky deep defense fits his game, if the line holds
nextGame.body:
New Orleans is close to the ideal opponent for this profile. It ranks last in deep-pass EPA allowed and 27th in explosive pass rate, and it gives up 274.6 passing yards a game to quarterbacks, 29th in the league. Lead receivers have beaten their usual output against the Saints by 3.3 PPR points a game, and top tight ends have found 0.44 EPA per target. That is the McMillan-and-Waller intermediate game Young lives on. The catch is the pass rush: the Saints' sack rate ranks seventh, which goes straight at his biggest weakness. The game is indoors, the Book has it near a pick'em with the Saints -1.5, and the total of 47.5 leans toward a game where he keeps throwing.

Availability tilts both ways. Carolina is without guard Damien Lewis, who has played 89% of snaps, with fellow guard Brady Christensen still on IR. That leaves an interior line thinner against a front that gets home. Xavier Legette has been designated to return from IR, which would give Young a third outside option if he is activated. On the other side, the Saints are losing center Erik McCoy "for a little bit." Travis Etienne Jr. remains on IR and CJ Donaldson is out, so their backfield and line are depleted. That should limit how long they can sustain drives, but it hardly guarantees a run-heavy game that shortens Young's day.

keyMatchups.title: His intermediate game vs. a broken secondary
keyMatchups.body: Young's best throws travel past 10 yards, and New Orleans has allowed more EPA on deep passes than anyone. If he gets the time to push the ball, this is the setup for a Week 1 or Week 4-style day. The Saints' deep numbers are bad enough that even some regression keeps them a target.

keyMatchups.title: Saints rush vs. a patched interior
keyMatchups.body: New Orleans gets sacks, and Carolina is down a starting guard with another on IR. Young has already taken his share of sacks this year. Long third downs are where his games go sideways, so early-down success matters more than usual here.

keyMatchups.title: McMillan and Waller in favorable spots
keyMatchups.body: Lead receivers have run well above their averages against this defense, and tight ends have been efficient against it too. McMillan and Waller are Young's two most efficient high-volume targets. Funneling the ball to them over the middle is the cleanest path.

nextGame.watch: His intended air yards: if he is pushing the ball around 10 yards downfield like his good games, he should feast; if the Saints' rush drives it toward the Tampa and Green Bay levels, expect sacks and checkdowns.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume is safe. Carolina throws more than almost anyone, and its defense will keep forcing it to, so something like 240 to 285 passing yards a game is a reasonable band even if efficiency slips. The intermediate and middle-of-the-field production looks like genuine growth, given the career-best bad-throw rate, but the deep completion rate on a few dozen attempts will cool. The touchdown rate, strong for him, leans on a red-zone line with 12 touchdowns despite poor success there, and that is the part most likely to come down.

The sacks are the swing. With Lewis out and his pressure-to-sack rate trending the wrong way, expect roughly three to four sacks a game and the occasional floor game against strong fronts. Overall, he projects as a high-volume, middle-efficiency starter: closer to his season line than to his last three games, with spikes against soft secondaries.
swingFactors: Interior line health with Lewis out
Whether the intermediate/deep efficiency holds as the sample grows

confidence.note: Eight games of clear growth backed by his career trend, but the deep split is small and form has swung week to week.
